summary: Clarifies the GMPLS signaling procedures for controlling the label used on the output interface of the egress node of a Label Switched Path, known as Egress Control.

plainLanguage.summary: It explains who decides which door a path should use when it reaches the very last stop.

subtitle: Clarifying how the final hop in a label-switched path controls which label to use.

tldr.problem: In GMPLS (Generalized MPLS), when a label-switched path reaches the egress node (last hop), it was unclear how the egress node should decide which label to use on the output interface.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC clarifies that the head-end node can specify the egress output interface and label in the Explicit Route Object (ERO). The egress node examines the ERO to find interface and label information, checking the U-bit (upstream flag) to distinguish unidirectional from bidirectional paths.
tldr.outcome: Egress Control procedures are now explicit in GMPLS signaling, allowing head-end routers to control label usage at path endpoints. This clarification updates RFC 3473 without changing mechanisms.

today: RFC 4003 clarifies egress control procedures in GMPLS signaling as a Proposed Standard. It remains relevant for MPLS and GMPLS implementations that need to control label usage at path egress points.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Egress Control refers to a router's ability to control which label is used on the output interface of the final hop (egress node) of a Label Switched Path (LSP). This was an early requirement in GMPLS design. The procedures for egress control were generalized as GMPLS evolved, but the specification became unclear. This RFC clarifies the procedures without modifying GMPLS mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: When a packet travels from router A through intermediate routers to router Z, router A should be able to tell router Z which exit door to use and what label to put on the data.

sections.title: Egress Control Procedures
sections.content: The head-end node controls egress behavior by placing information in the Explicit Route Object (ERO). When the egress node processes the ERO, it checks whether the ERO specifies an outgoing/downstream interface. If it does, the node examines the label subobject that follows. The U-bit (upstream bit) in the subobject indicates whether the label is for the forward direction (U-bit clear) or upstream traffic (U-bit set). For unidirectional LSPs, one label is examined; for bidirectional LSPs, two labels are examined.
sections.plainLanguage: The starting router uses a special field to say: 'Send traffic out this interface with this label.' The egress router checks a bit flag to know if the label is for forward or backward traffic.

sections.title: Recording and Error Handling
sections.content: If the egress node is recording the path taken (RRO, or Route Record Object), it should include both the specified interface information and the selected label or labels in the RRO response. If the ERO contains labels that the egress node cannot support or accept, the node SHOULD generate a PathErr message with error code 'Routing Error' and error value 'Bad Explicit Route Object'. These procedures are consistent with RFC 3473 GMPLS signaling.
sections.plainLanguage: If keeping records, the egress router notes which interface and label it ended up using. If it can't use what the starting router asked for, it sends an error message.
